_about: One robot description, two consumers: the TypeScript world builds the body from it, the Java RobotConfig reads the same file.
name: box-v1

chassis._source: cited: ROBOT_BUILD.md, the build this simulator is FOR. Section 4.1 gives the footprint as 15.5 (X, fore-aft) x 17.5 (Y) in with bumpers and the top plate at Z 11.625; section 4.2 puts the axles at X +-5.5, Y +-6.75 (wheelbase 11.0, track 13.5) on goBILDA 96 mm mecanums; section 12 totals 14.4 kg with the CG 5.9 in up and +0.3 in forward. WAS a 16.93 in SQUARE box at 14 kg with the CG 50 mm below centre, described in its own note as 'a typical 18 in FTC box robot' -- a placeholder, not this robot. The real one is not square: the extra width is the intake mouth and the shorter length buys the intake 2.5 in at the front and the trough 3.5 in at the back.

drivetrain.maxSpeed_mps_source: POLICY, and 0 means no cap, which is the shipping default -- the robot is allowed everything it has. It exists because a shot is refused in m/s, not in stick percent: charging the mouth faster than the ball's own horizontal speed leaves no launch under the hood's 80 deg stop, so at 1.7 m/s the robot cannot shoot inside 50 in at all and fires from 60 in out (tools/frontcheck.ts). Set this to drive a match at a speed that stays shootable. Verified by tools/topspeed.ts, which reports the peak as well as the settled speed because a limiter that only holds in the steady state still lunges past it on every launch.
drivetrain.freeSpeed_mps_source: MEASURED. The drive motor's free speed through its gearing times the wheel radius comes to 2.19 m/s, and 2.19 is also the fastest speed observed in any run (tools/frontcheck.ts). Note that tools/topspeed.ts reports only 1.98 forward and 2.01 strafing and says so as a LOWER BOUND, not a contradiction: the longest clear straight this field has is 2.7 m and the robot is STILL ACCELERATING at the boards. There is no longer clear line to use -- the corner-to-corner diagonal looks like 4.6 m and goes through both HIVEs, and measuring it reads 1.69, which is the collision and not the drivetrain. 2.19 is the value set, and it is corroborated twice: it is what the drive motor's free speed through its gearing times the wheel radius comes to, and it is the fastest speed observed in any run (tools/frontcheck.ts, which gets a longer effective runway than this tool can). The UI derived the same 2.19 independently and now reads this field instead, so there is one number rather than three. It feeds the cap's open-loop half -- without it the governor can only react to a robot that is already too fast, and a 0.80 m/s cap peaked at 1.29. Erring HIGH here costs a few percent of the asked-for speed and erring low lets the robot lunge, so the high observation is the right one to take. RE-MEASURE after any change to wheel radius, gear ratio, mass or rollingRes_N; on a real robot it falls with the battery, which is what the feedback half is for.
drivetrain._source: cited: ROBOT_BUILD.md section 4.2 -- four goBILDA 5203-2402-0014 (13.7:1, 435 rpm, 384.5 CPR at the wheel) direct-driving 96 mm mecanums, axles at X +-5.5 and Y +-6.75. WAS the 312 rpm variant on a 13.0 in square wheelbase, which is why this simulator measured a 1.56 m/s top speed against the build's own 2.19 m/s free and 2.14 loaded (section 4.2). Every speed measurement taken before 2026-09-19 was taken on a slower robot than the one being built.

intake.rollerRadius_m_source: guess: a 2.75 in compliant wheel, the usual FTC intake roller - CALIBRATE
intake.rollerMu_source: guess: durometer-35 compliant wheel on a moulded plastic ball. Caps the force the roller can put into a ball - CALIBRATE
intake.squeeze_N_source: guess: how hard the roller is preloaded onto the ball by sitting below ball height. This is the normal load that makes the friction cap non-trivial - CALIBRATE

hopper._source: G407: a ROBOT may not CONTROL more than 4 SCORING ELEMENTS at once. WAS 6, which put every cycle time, shot rate and autonomous ball budget in this repository on a robot that would be penalised. This is a rule, not a design parameter. The indexer's old inability to feed from a nearly empty bin (docs/DECISIONS.md) made 4 look unusable; with indexLift at 0.6 it feeds, and tests/shoot.test.ts fires 12 in 23 s from a 4-ball bin against 11 in 67 s from a 6-ball one. tools/movingfire.ts tops up to this number rather than to 7.

shot.patrolHalfAngle_deg_source: MEASURED by tools/releasecheck.ts --pathcap, which drives the sector and shoots while it does. It is HOW FAR ROUND THE OPENING THE DRIVER SHOULD GO, not a gate: the shot gate is turret.fireOpenCap_deg and it is untouched at 60. The two are different questions -- the cap says where a shot is still allowed, this says where it is still worth being. WHY IT LOOKS LIKE IT SHOULD MATTER: with every gate lifted and a perfect robot, 260 shots split by bearing land 94% at 0-20 deg off the opening, 100% at 20-35, 89% at 35-50 and 8% at 50-65, because the far band is where the aperture is half shut (cos 55 = 0.57) AND where the robot is reversing. ON THE REAL ROBOT IT LARGELY DOES NOT, and an earlier 4-seat sample that said otherwise did not replicate. 9 seeds, about 130 balls a row, stock robot, real noise, pocket filling, asked 1.5 m/s: +-35 deg lands 68% at 1.23 s per ball IN (0.91 m/s achieved); +-45 lands 71% at 1.01 s (0.95 m/s); +-60 lands 69% at 1.14 s (0.99 m/s). The LAND RATES are indistinguishable -- per-seed spreads are 53-85%, far wider than the 3 points between the rows -- so the earlier claim of +7 points at +-45 was noise. What survives is the timing: +-45 is about 11% faster per scored ball than +-60 and 18% faster than +-35, and +-35 is the worst of the three because a shorter pass is proportionally more reversing and the achieved speed falls. SET TO 35 BY PREFERENCE, not by measurement; 45 is the fastest row. Neither is settled at this sample size and about 300 balls a row would decide it. Drawn on the floor by the Patrol zone overlay so it is a place rather than a number.

transfer.cycleTime_s_source: RE-MEASURED 2026-09-19 on tools/zonerun.ts, whose rocker TIPS -- which matters, because a pocket that fills is exactly what makes a fast cycle look bad and the old harness never emptied one. 60 s x 2 seeds, patrolling the sector, balls CREDITED per second: 0.5 s -> 1.19/s at 61% landed; 0.6 s -> 0.97/s at 55%; 0.8 s -> 0.80/s at 56%; 1.0 s -> 0.70/s at 63%. Land RATE barely moves across the range and throughput nearly doubles, so the rate is the wrong thing to optimise: 0.6 s scores 39% more per second than 1.0 s did. 0.6 s is also the mechanism's own floor (PHYSICS Appendix B: elevator 0.26 + gate 0.08 + margin), so 0.5 s is not offered however well it measures. WAS 1.0, chosen on tools/movingtune.ts --cycle where the pocket never tipped and a fast cycle was penalised for a pile the game would have emptied. RE-MEASURED 2026-09-18 by tools/movingtune.ts --cycle on the one-branch table with the measured band, pooled over every case: 0.6 s fires 1.12/s and lands 83% (13 wild) for 0.93 landed/s; 0.8 s 0.91/s at 88% for 0.80 landed/s; 1.0 s 0.81/s at 90% for 0.72 landed/s; 1.2 s 88%; 1.5 s 96% for 0.49 landed/s. The pocket, not the transfer, sets the pace: faster than about 0.8 s the next ball meets the last one still settling and the wild count climbs. 1.0 s is kept as the setting that holds 90%; 0.8 s is the throughput option at 2 points of land rate. MEASURED end to end by tools/movingtune.ts --cycle, not taken from the mechanism alone. The TRANSFER can do 0.6 s (PHYSICS Appendix B: elevator 0.26 + gate 0.08 + margin) and that is what it was set to first, but the POCKET cannot absorb balls that fast: flight is about 1.1 s, so at 0.6 s the next ball arrives while the last one is still settling and clips it. Swept, pooled over every driving case: 0.6 -> 81% in at 1.14 landed/s, 0.8 -> 86% at 0.99, 1.0 -> 91% at 0.85, 1.2 -> 91% at 0.67, 1.5 -> 100% at 0.65. 1.0 is the fastest setting that still lands nine of ten, and it scores 25% more per second than the 1.5 it replaced. Re-measure after any change to the pocket geometry or the entry model, which is what sets how long a ball takes to settle.
transfer._source: design parameter - the knob this project exists to explore
transfer.beltRadius_m_source: guess: the drive pulley on the feed belt. Belt speed is motor omega times this, and the belt has to beat gravity to lift a ball up the shaft - CALIBRATE
transfer.indexLift_source: How much of the indexer's push acts upward. A real indexer is a wheel pressed against the ball with its contact patch BELOW the ball's centre, so it lifts as much as it shoves. At 0 -- a purely horizontal shove, which is what this was -- a ball resting on the bin floor is pinned by its own floor contact and does not move at all, so balls only reached the magazine when something else shook them there. Sweep it before trusting the value: the working window measured in the sister build is 0.3-0.8, with 0 and 0.1 feeding nothing and 1.0 throwing balls out of the bin.
transfer.boreSize_m_source: derived, 3.80 in: passes a 3.62 in NECTAR and refuses two POLLEN, whose DIAGONAL is 2.8*sqrt(2) = 3.96 in. The window is [3.62, 3.96) and this sits in the middle of it. WAS 3.20 in (one POLLEN plus 0.4), on the argument that a NECTAR-sized bore is 4.1 in and two POLLEN fit side by side in 4.1 in -- true, but the binding number is the diagonal, not 5.6 in of side-by-side. Two consequences, both measured: the simulator could not admit a NECTAR at all, so it could not shoot the ball worth 2.5 points in the HIVE and the entire endgame in the FLOWERS (PHYSICS 9.12); and 0.2 in of clearance let a POLLEN entering crooked wedge in the doorway BELOW entryY, which leaves entryBusy true for ever -- the indexer admits nothing more and the belt cannot free what is stuck. On seed 43 that left one ball at -2.23 in with the belt driving and the gate cycling and shots 0 for the whole run; at 3.80 in the same seed fires normally. That is 9.13 and 9.14 as well - CALIBRATE against the real tube once it exists.
transfer.leadLatency_s_source: MEASURED by tools/movingfire.ts --gate. The exit speed is chosen when the gate is commanded and the ball leaves after the feed pulse and the wheel's lag, so under acceleration the shot carries a correction for a velocity the robot has grown out of; leading on v + a*tau predicts the velocity AT RELEASE instead. Deadbanded where a*tau stops being worth more than the flywheel encoder can resolve (one count over a 20 ms window is 107 rpm), because it differentiates a velocity and a standing robot jitters -- applied unconditionally it cost a stationary rig a third of its shots. WAS 0.30, tuned when the lead spent its whole correction on the flywheel and the flywheel therefore lagged badly. The lead solves the hood now, the hood is fast, and there is little stale target left to predict: on the shuttling case 0, 0.15 and 0.30 all land the same 0.36 per second, and 0.30 has the WORST downrange bias of the three (-27 cm against -7 and -5). 0.15 is best or tied on every column, so it is set there, but the honest summary is that this knob no longer moves the answer. Kept because a real feed is slower than this modelled one and a real hood servo will lag in a way this one does not - CALIBRATE tau against a real feed once one exists.

turret.range_deg_note: +-270 is 540 deg of travel: a turn and a half, so every bearing is reachable two ways over HALF the circle instead of over a 5 deg sliver. That width is the whole point. At +-185 the two wraps of a solution are both in range only within 5 deg of the stops, so the axis has no choice to make anywhere else -- the moment a turning chassis walks the bearing off the end, the only way back is a 360 deg traverse, 1.38 s at 261 deg/s with the muzzle sweeping the entire field on the way. MEASURED by tools/aimwatch.ts over 60 s of ordinary driving, three seeds: at +-185 the muzzle sits more than 45 deg off our own CELL 12.7% of the time and nearer the OPPONENT's than ours 16.8%; at +-270 that is 2.1% and 10.3%. Nothing else came close -- a 900 deg/s axis at +-185 still reads 6.4%, and capping the turn buttons to a quarter reads 5.0% and makes the robot a barge. The two CELLs are 25.5 in apart on one rocker (hive.redX_m -12.7 in, blueX_m +12.8 in), about 23 deg of separation at 60 in, which is why pointing a foot wide is not a near miss but the other alliance's goal.
turret.range_deg_source: design parameter, and a WIRING decision rather than a structural one: 540 deg of travel needs the turret's leads to survive a turn and a half, which is a service loop sized for it or a slip ring (a 12-circuit capsule is the usual FTC-legal part). WAS +-185, chosen when the argument was only 'more than a full turn so every bearing is reachable' -- true, and not enough: reachable ONE way means the axis is committed the instant it gets there. CALIBRATE against the real turret's cable stack before committing to 540.
turret.speed_dps_source: derived, PHYSICS Appendix B: an Axon MAX+ free-runs at 522 deg/s and the turret is 2:1 off it, so 261. WAS 180, back when the turret was a motor; at 180 a swing across the +-175 travel takes two seconds and the aim is still arriving when the shot wants to go. R502 allows 8 W and the MAX+ draws 7.59 - CALIBRATE against the real head.
turret.accel_dps2_source: derived, PHYSICS Appendix B: 6.7 N.m over a 0.031 kg.m^2 head, servo-response limited. WAS 900, which is a motor's figure and made the axis spend most of a swing accelerating - CALIBRATE from the real turret's step response.
turret.fireOpenCap_deg_source: MEASURED by tools/movingtune.ts --open. The mouth is a SLOT, so what a ball has to fit through is the opening seen edge-on: 14 in of depth becomes 14*cos(off-axis), which is 9.9 in at 45 deg, 6.6 at 62 and 3.6 at 75 -- for a 2.8 in ball. 75 was a geometric guess, on the reasoning that the aperture only vanishes at 90, and it is far too generous. Swept on the fast cases: at 75 they land 52% with 69 wild shots and a downrange group of +-76 cm; at 60 they land 100% with NOTHING wild and +-8 cm. Below 60 the cases here are placed outside it and cannot be measured, so 60 is the loosest setting that was actually clean, not a proven optimum - RE-MEASURE with cases placed nearer the normal if a tighter cap is ever wanted.
turret.fireLeadCap_deg_source: MEASURED by tools/zonerun.ts --cap, patrolling the shooting sector at speed with the latch on and the real rocker, 60 s x 2 seeds a cell. At 0.80 m/s: cap 20 lands 88% of 8 shots (0.06 balls/s, 89% of loops refused for the cap); 30 lands 87% of 15 with one wild; 45 lands 94% of 16 at 0.13 balls/s; no cap is identical to 45. At 0.84 m/s: 20 gives 0.06 balls/s, 30 gives 83%, 45 gives 92% of 24 at 0.23 balls/s, no cap identical. At 0.62 m/s: 20 gives 84%, 30 and up 92%. WAS 20, measured by tools/movingtune.ts --lead on the lead that looked the row up 0.15 s ahead and the table that zigzagged between branches (docs/DECISIONS.md 2026-09-18); those were what made a 25 deg lead miss, and movingtune's cases never reach 12 deg of lead so it could not re-measure it. Past 45 the outrun and hood-travel gates take over, which is why no cap reads the same. RE-MEASURE with zonerun --cap after any change to the lead, the table or the hood's travel.
turret.fireYawCap_dps_source: MEASURED by tools/movingtune.ts --spin, and it corroborates STRATEGY.md 7.2's 60 deg/s from a completely different direction. Spinning on the spot with the cap lifted: 0.18 stick (about 48 deg/s) lands 97% with nothing wild, 0.25 (about 66) lands 100%, 0.35 (93 deg/s, measured) collapses to 75% with 4 wild of 16 and a downrange spread of +-88 cm. The mechanism is the commit window: the feed is committed about 0.4 s before the ball leaves and a yawing chassis drags the turret's setpoint for all of it, so the error at RELEASE is the yaw rate times that delay. The readiness check on turret error cannot see it -- the axis is on target when the shot is committed and behind when it goes. 70 admits everything that measured clean and refuses what did not. RE-MEASURE if the turret gets faster or the feed shorter: the cap is the ratio of the two.
turret.aimGimbal_source: The turret is a GIMBAL: it should lock onto the goal and hold, not hunt. The aim is re-solved every loop from a localizer carrying 0.5 in and 0.5 deg of noise, so the raw solution jitters with the robot parked -- commanded straight through, the axis never settled and every shot left while the head was still moving. The deadband is set just under the launch yaw scatter (1.0 deg): below that there is nothing worth chasing, because a quarter degree of aim is invisible next to a degree of scatter. The filter takes per-frame noise out without lagging a real slew, since the bearing to a fixed goal moves on the timescale of the robot's own driving - CALIBRATE both against a real turret and a real odometry pod.
turret.muzzleHeight_m_source: cited: ROBOT_BUILD.md section 8.2, 15.8 in, which is also what PHYSICS Appendix B carries. WAS 0.28 m -- and 0.28 is INSIDE the chassis collider, whose top sits at 0.32 m. Robot.exitPoint() then walked every ball 6 cm up the shot line to spawn it clear of the box, so the world launched from 5.6 cm higher than the muzzle the SHOT TABLE was solved at. tools/aimbias.ts priced the disagreement exactly: the solver said -3.8 cm and the world put the ball +10.7 cm long, a 14.5 cm gap it attributed to 'launch geometry: muzzle height and offset'. Above the chassis top exitPoint is a no-op and the two agree by construction - CALIBRATE against the built shooter.
turret._accelSource: guess: 900 deg/s^2 reaches the 180 deg/s slew limit in 0.2 s, which is what a 5203-117 through a 2:1 reduction does against a turret of a few hundred g.cm^2. Derive it properly from motor torque over turret MOI once the real turret exists - CALIBRATE

hood._angleRangeSource: derived: the shot table the CORRECTED pocket asks for spans hood 41-76 deg over 30-150 in (arrival 32 deg down at 3.6 m/s, apex 66 in mean), so 40-80 covers it with margin and spends the servo's resolution on the range actually used. WAS 30-85, chosen by tools/hoodsweep.ts against a pocket tilted 11 deg too steep, which is why the old table sat at 75-85 deg lobbing balls in nearly vertically.
hood.tolDeg_source: DERIVED from what the wheel is already allowed to be wrong by. The readiness gate accepts flywheel.tolRpm = 60 rpm, which is worth about +-21 cm of range; 1 deg of hood is 3.5 cm of range (tools/fixedspeed.ts), so 60 rpm is about 6 deg of hood and a 2 deg window sits well inside the error already tolerated. It costs almost nothing to wait for -- the lead moves the hood 8.0 deg per m/s of radial speed and the servo does 120 deg/s, so a full-speed run's whole correction arrives in about 0.13 s against a 1.5 s cycle, and tools/movingfire.ts sees this gate close on under 1% of loops. It exists because the motion lead SOLVES the hood: before that the hood only ever held the table's stationary angle and arrived long before the wheel did, so nothing checked it - CALIBRATE against a real servo, which will be slower and may need this loosened.
hood._sweepNote: PLAN.md's default was [30,60]. At that range every solution arrives still CLIMBING at 20-40 deg, threads the mouth and rebounds off the far wall: 19 usable ranges, best speed margin 8.0%. Extending the top of the range to 85 deg lets the ball drop in at 85 deg: 25 usable ranges covering 30-150 in, best margin 14.8% at 75 in. Re-run the sweep if the shooter geometry changes.

flywheel.rangeLead_s_source: MEASURED, and the answer is ZERO. It was 0.15 s, measured by tools/movingtune.ts --rangelead when it looked the WHOLE row up ahead; that measurement was of the wheel's lag plus the row shift together, and the row shift was the larger and the wrong-signed of the two (tools/flightcheck.ts, 2026-09-18: closing at 0.5 m/s from 52 in, 6.6 cm low with the led row). With the lead applied to the wheel target alone and re-swept, 176 pooled shots a step: 0 s lands 91% with the wheel 2 rpm off at release; 0.15 s 86%, 0.30 s 87%, 0.40 s 87%, 0.55 s 86%. The wheel does not lag enough to anticipate: two 5202s on 3.9e-4 kg.m^2 slew 1100 rpm/s against a target moving 140 rpm/s at 0.5 m/s. The look-ahead code stays, at zero, for a heavier or slower wheel -- RE-MEASURE if the flywheel inertia or motor count changes.
flywheel.encoderTicksPerRev_source: cited: a REV-11-1271 Through Bore reads 8192 counts a revolution, and on the wheel shaft through a 4:1 reduction that is 2048 counts per WHEEL revolution. WAS the 5202's own 28-tick motor encoder, and that is what made the readiness gate a coin flip: the hub reports velocity as a whole number of counts over its 20 ms window, so 28 ticks a rev is a 107 rpm lattice -- and with tolRpm at 60 the readiness WINDOW WAS NARROWER THAN ONE COUNT. Whether the robot fired came down to where that lattice happened to fall against the target, which is why it sat at 'FIRING' with the feedforward already dead on. At 2048 a rev one count is 1.5 rpm, so a tight window means something - CALIBRATE the reduction against the real shaft.
flywheel.motorCount_source: PHYSICS 9.19 and 9.21, and Appendix B. One motor slews the wheel at 462 rpm/s (tools/slew.ts), so reaching the table's 2315 rpm from rest takes FIVE SECONDS -- long enough that the robot reads as broken, and the reason the shooter spends most of a match 'spinning up'. Two motors give 794 rpm/s. The last commit measured the second motor as what makes the RECEDING case possible at all (0.00 -> 0.24 landed per second) and it is not a substitute for the flywheel inertia, nor the inertia for it: inertia fixes the per-shot dip, motors fix the chase. THE PORT IS PAID FOR by moving the turret to a servo (R502 allows 8 W; an Axon MAX+ is 7.59 W), which is what the hardware map below now says -- without that this is a nine-motor robot and R503 allows eight. tests/rules.test.ts counts it.
flywheel.I_fly_kgm2_source: A 96 mm goBILDA grip wheel (105 g, 1.21e-4 kg.m^2) PLUS a 96 mm x 12 mm 6061 disc behind it: pi*r^2*t*2700 = 234 g, I = 0.5*m*r^2 = 2.70e-4, so 3.91e-4 together and 0.34 kg on the shaft. WAS THE BARE GRIP WHEEL, and no FTC shooter that works is built that way. At 1.21e-4 a single POLLEN takes 210 rpm out of the wheel on its way past (tools/shootercheck.ts), three and a half times the 60 rpm firing window, and the tachometer cannot even see it coming: the hub reports velocity quantised to about 107 rpm a count on a 28-tick encoder, filtered over 6 loops. Every wild shot in tools/_acc.ts was that gap -- fired with the true speed 367 +- 101 rpm under target while the filtered reading said it was fine. Adding inertia is the answer a team reaches for and it costs nothing in the motor budget, which matters here because the robot is already at FTC's 8-motor limit (4 drive, intake, transfer, flywheel, turret) and cannot have a second flywheel motor without giving one up. Spin-up goes from 0.74 s to 2.0 s, which is what a real shooter takes - CALIBRATE by weighing the actual wheel stack.
flywheel._dragSource: guess, sized so windage costs about 5% of stall torque at free speed; a bigger value simply caps the achievable RPM - CALIBRATE from a TuningFlywheel spin-up curve
flywheel._tolRpmSource: the hub velocity loop settles 50-90 RPM above target at these gains, so an 80 RPM window opened only intermittently; 120 RPM is about 3% at the typical 3700 RPM target - tighten it once the loop is calibrated on the real hub
flywheel._source: I_fly from Gecko 96mm (cited); k/lossFactor guesses - CALIBRATE.
flywheel._motorNote: PLAN.md's default was a 5203-1620 at 1:1, which tops out at v_exit = k*w*r = 0.45*169.6*0.048 = 3.7 m/s and cannot reach the HIVE from anywhere on the field. A bare 6000 RPM motor gives 13.6 m/s. A 2:1 step-up on the 1620, or a dual-wheel k of 0.90, would do as well.
flywheel.minLandProb_source: MEASURED, and set by what it COSTS rather than by what it sounds like. The shot is refused unless the robot computes at least this CALIBRATED chance of landing: P(exit speed inside the band that threads the mouth, from the FILTERED wheel speed) x P(pointing inside the mouth, from the current turret error and the launch yaw scatter) x P(a ball arriving like that stays in, from tools/entrycheck.ts), all through the measured curve in config/landcal.json. `npm run tool -- tools/movingfire.ts --sweep` prices it in BALLS PER SECOND, which is the side a per-shot land rate cannot see -- refusing a 60% shot only pays if a better one turns up inside the 1.5 s the refused cycle costs. At 0.70: 0.45 landed per second stopped at 90% of the shots taken, 0.55 closing at 100%, 0.35 shuttling at 100%. 0.80 and above takes the STOPPED case to zero. RE-MEASURE AFTER ANY SHOOTER CHANGE, and do not carry the old number over: it was 0.85 against the bare-grip-wheel flywheel and a noiseless localizer, and both of those moved. It is only meaningful against the landcal curve it was swept on.
flywheel.tolRpm_source: MEASURED by tools/trimsweep.ts against balls in the CELL. It cannot be read off a datasheet because the floor is the encoder: the flywheel runs 28 ticks a rev direct-driven, so the hub's 20 ms velocity window sees 26 counts at 2800 rpm and ONE COUNT is 107 rpm -- about 15 in of range by tools/apercheck.ts. A single reading cannot resolve 30 rpm, which is why rpmFilterFrames exists: six loops of moving average is what makes this window mean anything. 120 rpm is +-14.9 in against a hole 8.9 in deep, and measured worse than 60 at every setting tried.
flywheel.kSkV_source: MEASURED by tools/flywheeltune.ts --ff, which is TuningFlywheel run offline: hold a duty, wait for steady state, record the speed, least-squares fit duty = kS + kV*rpm over 0.2..0.9 duty. Worst residual 0.0037 duty across the range, so the wheel really is that linear. These REPLACE the generic kS = 0.03, kV = 1/freeRpm that genconstants.mjs used to derive: at 2800 rpm the guess asks for 0.497 duty against the measured 0.466, which parks the wheel about 190 rpm high -- far enough outside a 60 rpm readiness window that the robot fires NOTHING. kP is unchanged and only has to cover the dip a shot takes out of the wheel; re-fit all three against a real TuningFlywheel log - CALIBRATE.
flywheel.rpmFilterFrames_source: MEASURED by tools/trimsweep.ts: 1 loop 14.0%, 3 loops 18.3%, 6 loops 31.5% of balls scoring, on the arrival-counting metric that run used. Averaging the hub's velocity estimate costs lag and buys resolution, and one raw reading is quantised to about 107 rpm. FlywheelGate.java carries the same ring buffer so the hub does the same thing.

calibration._about: Field trims. These are what a team actually adjusts between matches: they correct the SHOT TABLE against the real robot without regenerating it, and the Analysis tab computes them from a collected run.
calibration.rangeTrim_in_source: RE-MEASURED 2026-09-19 by tools/releasecheck.ts --noscatter --emptycell after the feed race was fixed: the group sat +7 +-2 cm long standing at 40 in and +5 +-3 at 52 in, every shot, so the table's answer reaches 2-3 in past the mouth's centre. +2 in of trim moves it back onto the centre, which is the setting that keeps the most margin against a pile. WAS 2.0, MEASURED by tools/movingtune.ts --sweep, firing from a DRIVING robot and recording where each ball crossed the mouth plane. The group sat 3-4 cm long with a 10 cm spread; the brain looks the table up at (range - trim), so a positive trim asks for a shorter shot. Swept 0-6 in over 48 balls a step: 0 gave 92% and +3 cm, 2 gave 96% and -1 cm, 3 gave 90%, 5 gave 96% and -6 cm. 2 in is where the group is CENTRED, which is the setting that keeps its margin when anything else moves. RE-MEASURE after any change to the muzzle, the shot table or the entry model: this absorbs the residue of all three.
calibration.turretTrim_deg_source: measured: atan(mean lateral error / mean range) from a collected run. Subtracted from the commanded azimuth, so it also absorbs a turret encoder zero that is a degree off.

camera._about: The AprilTag camera. TURRET-MOUNTED, which tools/tagstudy.ts calls the single highest-value hardware decision available: the turret already tracks the CELL, so a camera bolted to it is pointing at the tag whenever the shooter is aimed, by construction. A chassis-mounted one sees a tag only when the driver happens to be facing the right way.
camera._source_optics: ASSUMED, not measured. 640x480 is what the FTC SDK AprilTag pipeline usually runs at and 60 deg is a typical horizontal FOV for a C920-class webcam at 4:3. Swap in the real camera's numbers before trusting any range figure - CALIBRATE.
camera._source_noise: ASSUMED. A well-lit, in-focus, square-on tag localises its corners to roughly a quarter pixel; a small, blurred or oblique one is far worse. 0.5 px is a deliberately unflattering middle, and every accuracy figure rests on it.
camera._source_tag: ASSUMED. The am-5888 panel measures 17.00 x 4.34 in in the CAD, so the printed tag fits inside 4.34 in and 4 in is the common FTC size. NOT confirmed against the manual.
camera._source_minTagPx: ASSUMED. Below about a dozen pixels across, tag decode rate falls off a cliff. This is a range cutoff, not a decode model.
camera._source_obliquity: Geometric rather than guessed: a planar tag seen at angle t presents cos(t) of its width, so past about 70 deg the short axis is too few pixels to fit a homography, and it is also where the CELL's own lip begins to occlude the panel.
camera._source_latency: ASSUMED. Capture plus the SDK's AprilTag pipeline at 640x480 is tens of milliseconds; 50 ms is a common measured figure on a Control Hub - CALIBRATE.

sensors._mountFrame: robot-local FTC convention: x forward, y left, z up (metres)

localizer.velFilterAlpha_source: MEASURED as the smallest filter that keeps the robot shooting once the odometry noise is modelled at all. The lead is built entirely on the reported velocity, so with vel_mps at 0.04 the raw reading jitters the lead azimuth, the turret chases the jitter, its tracking error never settles under the gate's 3 deg and three of the shoot tests fired nothing. One pole at alpha 0.25 on a 60 Hz loop is about 50 ms of lag for roughly a third of the noise. The thing being estimated moves on the timescale of the robot's own acceleration, which is tenths of a second, so 50 ms is cheap - RETUNE against a real puck, whose noise will not be Gaussian.

noise._source: guess, sized on a two-pod odometry puck (goBILDA Pinpoint class) rather than measured. WAS ALL ZEROS AND READ BY NOTHING: the brain was handed ground-truth position, heading AND velocity, so the motion lead -- which is built entirely on the reported velocity -- had never been tested against an estimate that could be wrong. vel_mps is the one that matters: a puck differentiates a quantised encoder, and differentiating is the noisiest thing on the robot. 0.04 m/s against a ball horizontal of about 2.3 m/s is about one degree of bearing, the same order as the launch yaw scatter already modelled. xy_in and heading_deg are a standing error rather than a drift, which flatters a real puck over a long match and is fair over the few seconds a shot takes - CALIBRATE by driving a known square and reading the closing error. The TARGET bearing and range are still exact, which is the bigger remaining lie: on a real robot they come from an AprilTag pipeline with its own noise and 50-100 ms of latency.

drift._about: INTEGRATED error, which is what odometry actually has. Before this the localizer was ground truth plus white noise -- half an inch of error forever, however far the robot drove -- and that made the AprilTag look optional, because there was no drift for it to correct.
drift.scaleErr_source: One sigma, drawn ONCE per run: a wheel diameter or pod spacing that is not quite the number typed in. 0.5% is 0.6 in over a 10 ft drive, one sign, and it never averages out - MEASURE by driving a surveyed 10 ft and comparing what the pods report.
drift.gyroBias_dps_source: One sigma, drawn ONCE per run. THE EXPENSIVE ONE: 0.1 deg/s is 3 deg after a 30 s AUTO, and heading error rotates every inch driven after it, so position error grows with DISTANCE and never comes back. A BHI260AP-class fused IMU (what a goBILDA Pinpoint carries) is around here - MEASURE by sitting still for 60 s and reading the heading off.
drift.gyroWalk_dps_source: Random walk on that bias, per root second. Keeps the bias from being a single constant a smart filter could learn and cancel outright - guess, CALIBRATE from a long stationary log.
drift.gyroNoise_dps_source: White noise on the rate. Averages out over a match and is the least important of the three - guess.
drift.slipFrac_source: Per-step position error as a fraction of the step, both axes: the wheel that breaks traction while the encoder counts through it. This is the term that does NOT average out and the one a dead-wheel pod exists to avoid, so it should fall a lot if the pods are unsprung and true - MEASURE by driving into the wall and reading the jump.

fuse._about: Tag fixes correcting the dead-reckoned pose. A fiducial at a SURVEYED position is a measurement of the OBSERVER before it is anything else, and this is what stops odometry drift growing without bound.
fuse.gain_source: Fraction of each fix's disagreement absorbed. A tag fix carries 4% of range -- 2 in at 50 -- so snapping onto every detection at 30 Hz injects that straight into the aim; a one-pole averages the noise down while still removing drift, which is one-signed. 0.15 is about a 7-fix time constant, a quarter second. RAISE it if drift is winning, LOWER it if the aim jitters - SWEEP against odometryErrorIn().
fuse.rejectOver_in_source: Refuse a fix that disagrees with the estimate by more than this. Three feet of disagreement between two frames is a misread, the wrong tag, or a pose that has already failed -- not drift, which arrives an inch at a time. A gate here is what stops one bad decode throwing the match away - guess, TIGHTEN once the real drift rate is measured.
fuse.headingGain_source: The same, off the tag's YAW, and much smaller because yaw carries an order more noise than bearing -- 6 deg of sigma against 0.5. At 0.05 the steady-state heading error is sigma*sqrt(g/(2-g)) = about 1 deg, which beats a gyro bias left to run for 30 s. THIS IS NOT OPTIONAL: a bearing-and-range fix is measured along a line drawn at the heading the robot believes, so correcting position under a heading that is 4 deg out drives the pose to a place consistent with the 4 deg. Measured with headingGain at 0 the correction made things WORSE -- 0.8 in of error became 7.2 - SWEEP with tools/driftcheck.ts.

tag._about: The tag pipeline. THIS BLOCK REPLACES AN ORACLE: `game.upCellAzimuthDeg` and friends used to come straight off the world with no noise, no latency, no field of view and no way to be invalid, and both brains aimed on them. docs/LOCALIZATION.md is the design; packages/core/src/physics/tagCamera.ts is the model.
tag.mount_source: docs/LOCALIZATION.md phase 4, and it is a hardware decision as much as a software one. A chassis camera with this lens covers 17% of headings, so 'a tag is in view' is luck; the turret already tracks the CELL, so a camera bolted to it is pointing at the tag whenever the shooter is aimed. Cost: the camera's wiring has to survive 370 deg of turret travel, same as the feed tube.
tag.fov_deg_source: cited, rounded down: a Limelight 3A is 63.3 deg horizontal and a C920 at 4:3 is 70.4. 60 is the conservative one - CALIBRATE against the lens actually fitted, and note the gate is against the TURRET angle, not the chassis.
tag.maxRange_in_source: guess, sized on a 4 in tag at 640x480 needing roughly 20 px across to decode reliably - MEASURE by walking the robot back until the detection rate falls off, because this number sets where the shot zone stops.
tag.maxIncidence_deg_source: guess. Past about 65 deg the tag's face has too little projected area to decode, and the pose it does return is the worst-conditioned one. docs/LOCALIZATION.md calls a tighter limit here the thing that would most change the answer - MEASURE it on the real tag before trusting any shot taken from the side.
tag.frameRateHz_source: cited: an FTC webcam through AprilTagProcessor at 640x480 runs 20-30 fps. Deliberately SLOWER than the 60 Hz control loop, because that gap is why a fix goes stale between shots and it is the gap the readiness gate now has to respect.
tag.latencyMs_source: docs/PHYSICS.md 6 named 50-100 ms as the real figure and the simulator had none of it. This is the slowest thing in the aim chain and the only one the robot cannot make faster by trying harder - MEASURE with the Limelight's own pipeline latency field, or by waving a tag past a known encoder angle.

noise._source: guesses, but their RATIO is the point and it is the well-documented shape of an AprilTag pose: bearing is the strong axis (the tag's centre is a sub-pixel centroid), range is an apparent-SIZE estimate so its error is a fraction of the range rather than a fixed distance, and tag YAW is the worst-conditioned axis by an order - which is unfortunate, because the 'is the mouth still open towards me' gate is built on yaw. CALIBRATE all three by parking the robot at a surveyed spot and logging detections.

target.holdS_source: guess. How long a fix may be carried forward on odometry before the target counts as lost and the turret starts sweeping. Long enough to ride out the blind window of a TIP and a couple of dropped frames; short enough that the carried fix has not drifted past the mouth - SWEEP it against landed-per-second once the odometry error is calibrated.
target.maxFireAgeS_source: MEASURED against the pipeline, not chosen: at 30 fps and 75 ms of latency a fix is 75-108 ms old the moment it arrives, so anything under about 0.12 s refuses every shot the camera can supply. 0.25 s leaves room for one dropped frame and no more. THIS IS THE GATE THAT REPLACES THE ORACLE'S `hiveTipping`: a rocker going over blinds the camera, the fix ages past this, and the robot holds fire without ever being told the hive moved.
target.scanRateDps_source: guess, well under the turret's 261 deg/s so the lens is not smearing while it sweeps. This is what the robot does with no fix at all, and it is why no field geometry is baked into the deliverable: it re-acquires from wherever it is rather than from where it was told it was - CALIBRATE against the frame rate, since a sweep faster than fov_deg*frameRateHz steps past tags without ever seeing one.
target.fireOnOdometry_source: Policy, not physics. With no tag in view the robot still knows where the HIVE is -- it does not move -- so odometry plus the baked mouth position gives a bearing and a range, and this says whether a shot may be taken on that alone. TRUE keeps the robot shooting when vision drops out, which is what a real team wants and what makes the camera an improvement rather than a single point of failure. THE RISK IS NOT THE POSITION, IT IS THE ROCKER STATE: odometry cannot see which CELL is up, so after a TIP nobody saw, the robot aims confidently at a mouth that is now facing the other way. The tag is the only thing that corrects that, which is why `stateFromTag` below refuses the shot until a tag has been seen at least once - SWEEP this against landed per second with the camera disabled before trusting it in a match.
target.anchorAlpha_source: OFF, and deliberately. A single sighting is one relative measurement between two unknowns -- where the robot is and where the HIVE is -- and it cannot pin both. `sensors.localizer.fuse` chooses to believe the SURVEY and estimate the ROBOT, which is the right way round because the field is built to a drawing and cad/parts.json has its geometry. Estimating the pivot from a pose that is itself corrected by the pivot is circular: the pair drifts off together, consistent with each other and wrong about the field, and no measurement ever notices. Set it non-zero ONLY with fuse.gain at 0, i.e. if you distrust the survey more than the odometry - it is a choice between the two, not a way to have both.
target.measAlpha_source: How much of each new detection to take into the target estimate. 1 replaces it outright, which is what this did first -- and it means the aim point jumps by that detection's own error, about 2 in at 50, thirty times a second. At 0.35 roughly five sightings are averaged and the noise comes down as their root, for about 90 ms of lag against a target that is not moving. A change of TAG ID bypasses this entirely and replaces the estimate: the two CELLs are 14 in apart across the pivot and an average of them aims at the rocker in between - SWEEP it against landed per second; it trades aim noise for staleness and the balance is not obvious.
target.maxStateAgeS_source: MEASURED by tools/tipcheck.ts. `fireOnOdometry` let a robot fire for ever on a tag it had decoded ONCE: the freshness test was `ageS <= maxFireAgeS || (fireOnOdometry && seenTag)`, and the second arm has no clock in it. That is defensible for a fix going briefly stale and indefensible across a TIP, which is the one event that changes which CELL is up AND hides the evidence -- the new tag faces the other way, so from the old shooting spot the camera simply stops decoding and the robot carries on aiming at a pocket that is now upside down. Measured: firing from 40 in, the hive went over at 10.6 s with 16 away and 12 credited, and the robot then fired 60 more balls over the next 35 s and credited NONE of them, reporting CLEAR TO FIRE throughout. Past this age the state is an assumption rather than a measurement, so the robot stops and sweeps for a tag instead. 1.5 s is about two feed cycles at 0.6 s: long enough to ride out the tag being blocked by its own ball in flight, short enough that a tip costs two wasted shots rather than sixty. RE-MEASURE if the cycle time or the camera's frame rate change.

hub._velocityPidSource: The /32767 scale is the hub's own, which is why f*maxTicksPerSec/32767 is about 1. Measured here on the flywheel settling inside its 80 RPM readiness window 5 s after the command: i=3 lands 186 RPM high, i=8 158 high, i=15 47 high (ready), i=25 20 high. 15 it is - CALIBRATE against a real TuningFlywheel log, and note that a team running its own feedforward + P loop (FlywheelGate) bypasses this entirely.
hub._source: guess - CALIBRATE against TuningDrive logs from a real hub

limits._source: R503: 'ROBOTS are limited to a total of 8 motors and 8 servos ... for all MECHANISMS used in all configurations.' maxServos WAS 12, on the grounds that two hubs give 12 ports. The number of ports is not the limit; the rule is, and ports only cap it further. Both numbers were in the spec type and read by nothing, which is how the 12 went in and how a nine-motor flywheel config reached the working tree; tests/rules.test.ts counts the hardware map against them now.
